Illini Speedster -
Along with his brother, Jim, he started his racing
career in hot rods in 1946 on the west coast near their
home at Alhambra. Drove hot rods and modified
stock cars here on the small track at state fair park
from 1948-50. First start in the 500 was in 1950 in
the City of Glendale Spl. built by A. J. Watson,
dubbed the "Pots and Pans Spl." because of limited
budget. Switched to NASCAR stock car circuit,
competing and winning many races through 1955.
Returned to Indianapolis speedway in 1956 qualify-
ing McNamara Spl., finishing fifth in the race. An
eye injury kept him out of the 1957, 500 miler after
he qualified the Sumar Spl. In 1958, he averaged
145.596 miles per hour to set a new four lap qualify-
ing record at Indianapolis. The first lap crash
that put 14 cars out of the race also involved Dick.
Finished third in the 200 mile big car grind here
last summer. Has appeared here many times in late
model stock cars. His biggest fans are wife, Carolyn
and daughter, Nancy, 3.

=== COLUMN 2 ===
The Men
CELE
CXk
Behind the Men
Behind the Wheel
Behind the success of each of the nationally-
known auto racers is the mechanic. A quiet
craftsman whose name never quite makes the
headlines, this little-known person toils long hours
in the quiet of his garage using every known
technique to make the machine he is working on
as near perfect as possible.
Each of these men likes to work with his hands.
And each is never quite satisfied with the finished
product. Theirs is a constant, burning curiosity
to learn more of the engines that they already
know down to the last minute nut and washer.
No detail is too small for these men. Experience
has taught them that malfunctioning little parts
can cause big trouble.
Men like Beckley, Watson, and Moore are not
only mechanics, they are skilled automobile en-
gineers and builders. They are truly artisans in
a sport that is replete with many men who proved
to be mechanical geniuses.
Men like Henry Ford, Fred and Augie Duesen-
berg, Harry Miller, Harry Stutz, Fred Offenhauser,
and others were mechanics. Their greatest joy
was tinkering with a high-speed engine trying to
coax more speed and better performance out of
these highly-temperamental power plants. Their
perseverance has resulted in better motor cars,
priced within reach of most Americans, which
has made our nation the leader in automobile
production in the world.

Tinley Park, III.
Born: September 12, 1916
Died: May 12, 1961
Indianapolis Speedway
Back in 1935, an 18 year old farm boy
pedalled his bicycle 35 miles from his home
at Tinley Park, Ill., to the one mile dirt
track at Roby, Ind., to watch the stars of
the American Automobile Association in
big car races there. That young man was
Tony Bettenhausen, who less than three
years later started his own career in racing
and who developed into the greatest auto
racer in the era of high speed modern cars.
Tony Bettenhausen is gone. And it is
a certainty that there never will be another
driver quite like him. Immensely popular
Photo Courtesy — USAC
with racing fans all over the country,
Tony's biggest romance was with the rac-
ing fans at state fair park. The large
German population took to the crew cut
of auto racing at state fair park which dates back 58 years.
Bettenhausen was tops as a driver. Of that there can be no question. He ranks fourth in the all time
national championship big car point ratings behind Earl Cooper, Tommy Milton and Ralph De Palma three
giants in racing history. His 21 national championship speedway big car victories puts him far ahead of all others
in the history of organized racing. He was national champion in 1951 and 1958 and only ten drivers have won
the national title more than once.
Tony was a man of many talents. A splendid driver ... a crack mechanic . .. an excellent after-dinner
speaker . .. a man with a ready wit. Tony
was all of these and more. He drove to
